#html:true
ANOVA (analysis of variance): purpose, required variable types, what a significant result does / does not show; possible patterns after rejecting $H_0$ (3 groups)
column2:
Compares means of one continuous (interval/ratio) DV (dependent variable) across groups of a nominal IV (independent variable, factor)
Tests all groups simultaneously → controls familywise error rate
Omnibus: shows an overall effect, not which groups differ → post-hoc needed
3 groups: 4 patterns (all differ; or one group differs from two equal groups, 3 ways)

column1: Familywise error rate: definition, formula, why it is a problem for multiple t-tests (k groups, $\alpha = .05$)
column2:
Error rate across multiple tests on the same data (experimentwise)
Each test carries 5% Type I risk → risks accumulate
$1-(1-\alpha)^m$ with $m = k(k-1)/2$ tests
3 groups → 3 tests: 14.3%; 5 groups → 10 tests: ≈ 40%

column1: One-way vs two-way ANOVA (analysis of variance): number of IVs (independent variables), null hypotheses tested
column2:
One-way: 1 IV (> 2 levels); $H_0: \mu_1 = \mu_2 = \dots = \mu_k$ (no group effect); $H_1$: at least one $\mu_i$ differs, not all
Two-way: 2 IVs (factors); 3 $H_0$s: main effect A, main effect B, A × B (no interaction)

column1: SSB (sum of squares between) vs SSW (sum of squares within): meaning, relation; why analysing variances tests means (one-way ANOVA)
column2:
SSB: differences due to treatment; distance of group means from grand mean
SSW: individual differences not explained by treatment; distance of data points from own group mean
$SST = SSB + SSW$
Means compared via the ratio of these two variance sources

column1: One-way ANOVA formulas: SSB (sum of squares between), SSW (sum of squares within), SST (total) (k groups, $n_i$ per group)
column2:
$SS_B = \sum_i n_i(\bar X_i - \bar X)^2$
$SS_W = \sum_i \sum_j (X_{ij} - \bar X_i)^2$
$SS_T = \sum (X_{ij} - \bar X)^2 = SS_B + SS_W$

column1: One-way ANOVA table: df (degrees of freedom), MS (mean squares), F-ratio and what each MS reflects (k groups, N total)
column2:
$df_B = k-1$; $df_W = N-k$; $df_T = N-1$
$MS = SS/df$
$MS_B$: how much group means differ from grand mean; $MS_W$: how much individuals vary around own group mean
$F = MS_B/MS_W$

column1: F-ratio interpretation, decision rule, reporting format (one-way ANOVA)
column2:
Large F: between-group > within-group variance → reject $H_0$
Small F: mostly within-group variance → fail to reject
Reject if $F_{obt} > F_{crit}(\alpha, df_B, df_W)$ or $p < \alpha$
Report: $F(df_B, df_W) = \dots, p = \dots$

column1: F-distribution properties; F-table layout
column2:
Positively skewed; values ≥ 0
Shape set by two df: $df_1$ (numerator), $df_2$ (denominator)
More symmetric as df increase
Table: $df_1 = k-1$ in columns, $df_2 = N-k$ in rows

column1: ANOVA assumptions and how each is checked
column2:
Independence of observations: from study design, not tested
Normality within each group (two-way: each cell): Shapiro–Wilk
Homogeneity of variances: Levene's test
Two-way: balanced design (equal n per cell) recommended

column1: Shapiro–Wilk vs Levene's test: $H_0$, p-value interpretation (ANOVA assumption checks)
column2:
Shapiro–Wilk: $H_0$ data normal; p > .05 → assumption met
Levene: $H_0$ equal variances across groups, $H_A$ at least one differs; p < α → assumption violated
Levene uses absolute deviations from group mean: $Z_{ij} = |X_{ij} - \bar X_i|$

column1: Alternatives to classical one-way ANOVA (unequal variances; non-normal data)
column2:
Unequal variances: Welch's ANOVA
Non-normal data: Kruskal–Wallis (non-parametric)

column1: $\eta^2$ (eta squared) in ANOVA: formula, meaning; vs partial $\eta^2$
column2:
$\eta^2 = SS_{effect}/SS_{total}$
Size of the effect (proportion of variance explained), not only significance
Partial $\eta^2 = SS_{effect}/(SS_{effect} + SS_E)$; ≥ $\eta^2$; identical in one-way designs

column1: Post-hoc tests: purpose, logic, when to run (ANOVA)
column2:
ANOVA says whether there is a difference; post-hoc says where
Pairwise independent-samples t-tests with adjusted significance level → familywise error controlled
Only after a significant omnibus F

column1: Tukey HSD (honestly significant difference) vs Bonferroni vs Scheffé post-hoc tests
column2:
Tukey: most common after one-way; all pairs; controls familywise error; best for balanced designs
Bonferroni: α / number of comparisons (e.g. .05/3 ≈ .017); more conservative, strict control
Scheffé: complex comparisons (not only pairwise); flexible, also conservative

column1: Tukey HSD (honestly significant difference) output: sign convention of the mean difference (statsmodels meandiff vs pingouin diff)
column2:
statsmodels: meandiff = mean(group2) − mean(group1); negative → group1 has the higher mean (e.g. slower RT, reaction time)
pingouin: diff = mean(A) − mean(B) → opposite sign for the same pair

column1: Main effect vs interaction: definitions, appearance in interaction plot (two-way ANOVA)
column2:
Main effect: effect of one factor averaged over the levels of the other
Interaction: effect of one factor depends on the level of the other
Plot: non-parallel lines suggest interaction; crossing lines = strong interaction; parallel = none

column1: Two-way ANOVA SS (sum of squares) decomposition and formulas (factors A, B)
column2:
$SST = SSA + SSB + SSAB + SSE$ → $SSE = SST - SSA - SSB - SSAB$
$SSA = \sum n_i(\bar X_{i\cdot} - \bar X)^2$
$SSB = \sum n_j(\bar X_{\cdot j} - \bar X)^2$
$SSAB = \sum\sum n_{ij}(\bar X_{ij} - \bar X_{i\cdot} - \bar X_{\cdot j} + \bar X)^2$

column1: Two-way ANOVA df (degrees of freedom) and F-ratios (a levels of A, b levels of B, N total)
column2:
$df_A = a-1$; $df_B = b-1$; $df_{A\times B} = (a-1)(b-1)$; $df_E = N-ab$; $df_T = N-1$
3 F-tests: $F = MS_{source}/MS_E$, all with error (within-cell) $MS_E$ as denominator
e.g. 3 × 2, N = 60: 2, 1, 2, 54

column1: Interpreting a significant interaction (two-way ANOVA)
column2:
Examine the interaction first
Main effects can mislead → interpret with caution (may hide that one factor's effect depends on the other, e.g. region effect driven by one task only)
Follow up with simple effects / post-hoc tests
Interpret in context
